summary: Describes how to send several differently encoded versions of the same media source in separate RTP streams, called simulcast, and how to signal this in SDP. The solution uses the RID mechanism to identify the streams. It is standards-track.

eli5.summary: A video sender makes a big, medium and small copy of the same video. Viewers with fast or slow connections each grab the copy that suits them. This document describes how to announce those copies.

questions: how to signal simulcast in sdp
what is a rid-id in sdp
how does an sfu choose a simulcast stream
subtitle: How a video sender announces several versions of the same source, and how SDP describes them.

tldr.problem: In multiparty conferencing, one sender must serve receivers with different screens, bandwidth and codecs, and a central server wants to adapt without re-encoding video.
tldr.mechanism: The sender sends several differently encoded RTP streams of one media source. A new media-level SDP attribute, a=simulcast, lists them by the rid-ids defined in RFC 8851, separately for send and receive.
tldr.outcome: A middlebox can pick which stream to forward to each receiver. Simulcast stays within one SDP media description and one RTP session, which limits per-stream QoS and multicast use.

today: RFC 8853 is a Proposed Standard published in January 2021. It is not obsoleted or updated by any other RFC listed in its metadata. It relies on the RID mechanism in RFC 8851.

sections.title: What Simulcast Is
sections.content:
Multiparty video-conference systems usually use central servers that receive an RTP stream from each participant and send a suitable set of streams on to the others. The participants have different capabilities, such as screen size, CPU, bandwidth and codec.

Simulcast is the act of simultaneously sending multiple different encoded streams of the same media source, for example one video source encoded with different codecs or image resolutions. This document focuses on sending those streams over RTP to an intermediary, which then chooses which stream or streams to forward. It defines the identification and grouping of the streams and the SDP signaling for them.

The scope is SDP offer/answer with RTP transport, in point-to-point sessions and in centralized multiparty sessions. Multicast and broadcast transport are out of scope.
sections.eli5: Imagine filming one birthday party and handing out a big photo, a medium photo and a tiny photo. The person in the middle then gives each friend the size that fits their phone.

sections.title: Why Send Several Copies
sections.content:
A central node can adapt the session for each receiver in two ways. It can transcode (decode and re-encode), which adapts closely but is computationally expensive, adds delay and needs access to the media. Or it can switch a subset of the received streams to each receiver, which is cheap and has little effect on quality, but is harder to fit exactly to a receiver. Simulcast supports the switching approach, at the price of the sender using more network resources.

The RFC gives three use cases. Receivers can differ in codec, sampling (resolution and frame rate for video) and bitrate. A sender can reach receivers that support at most 360p and others that support 720p by sending both. Conferencing systems often show the active speaker large and do not send a speaker's own media back to them, so the previous active speaker is needed both large and small. And receivers may state preferences that conflict, which several streams can satisfy.

The number of simulcast streams is mainly limited by the processing and uplink capacity of the sender.
sections.eli5: If one friend wants a big picture and another wants a tiny one, it is easier to hand over ready-made copies than to redraw the picture for each friend.

sections.title: The a=simulcast Attribute
sections.content:
The RFC defines a new media-level attribute, a=simulcast. It builds on the Restriction Identifier (RID) mechanism of RFC 8851, where each a=rid line names a stream with a rid-id and can restrict things like bitrate, resolution, frame rate or the RTP payload types it may use.

The attribute has one or two parts, send and recv, each a list of simulcast streams. Streams are separated by a semicolon, and alternative formats for one stream are separated by a comma. In a=simulcast:send 1;2,3 recv 4, the sender offers two streams: the first follows rid-id 1, and the second can be sent as rid-id 2 or rid-id 3. It wants to receive one stream following rid-id 4.

A rid-id can be prefixed with ~ to mark that stream as initially paused. This requires RTP stream pause/resume support from RFC 7728 on the same media description.

Other rules: the attribute is media-level only, a session-level use MUST NOT be generated and MUST be ignored, and each media description MUST contain at most one a=simulcast line. The order of the streams in the send direction is a preference order, most preferred first, and so is the order of alternatives. A single rid-id MUST NOT appear more than once on the line.
sections.eli5: The line is like a menu note: "I can send picture 1, and picture 2 or 3, and I would like to get picture 4." Semicolons separate pictures, and commas offer a choice.

sections.title: Offer and Answer Rules
sections.content:
An offerer that wants simulcast SHALL include one a=simulcast attribute in the media description, and MUST be ready to receive any of the receive-direction streams and alternatives it listed.

An answerer that does not understand simulcast simply drops the attribute, as normal SDP offer/answer rules say. An answerer that does support it reverses the direction, so send becomes recv and the other way round. It MAY remove alternatives it dislikes and MAY reduce the number of streams, but it MUST NOT add streams or add alternatives that were not in the offer. If it sees several a=simulcast lines in one media description, it disables simulcast by removing them all.

The offerer then follows the answer. With no a=simulcast in the answer, or no rid-id in a direction, it MUST NOT use simulcast there. If rid-ids were removed, it can release the matching resources and MUST NOT send those streams.

Initially paused streams are handled with care: an answerer must not mark streams paused if the offer lacked pause/resume capability, and a paused stream in the offer SHOULD stay paused in the answer unless there is good reason. In later offers inside a session, the pause marks in the send direction are only informational, and the RFC 7728 signaling wins in a conflict.
sections.eli5: It is like ordering from a menu. The cook can say "we do not have that one" and cross items off, but cannot add dishes you never asked for.

sections.title: Signaling Examples
sections.content:
The RFC walks through a four-party conference with a central mixer. In the first example, Alice's client sends two H.264 streams, one for 1280x720 and one for 320x180, and wants to receive one 1280x720 stream. The only thing that marks simulcast is the line a=simulcast:send 1;2 recv 3. The server's answer reverses the directions: a=simulcast:recv 1;2 send 3.

The second example is Fred's two-camera client, which uses BUNDLE and several codecs. It offers H264-SVC, H264 and VP8, uses alternatives such as ~4,3 for the third stream of the first source, and starts lower-quality streams paused. The third example combines simulcast with redundancy, using redundant audio data, flexible FEC and RTP retransmission.

These examples show that a small number of RTP payload types can serve many simulcast streams, because the rid-id, not the payload type, tells the streams apart.
sections.eli5: The examples are sample order forms. One shows a simple order with two sizes, and the others show fancier orders with backup copies in case some get lost.

sections.title: How Streams Look on the Wire
sections.content:
Simulcast RTP streams MUST be related through the RtpStreamId source description item (RFC 8852), as the rid-ids on the SDP line say. With BUNDLE (RFC 8843), the MID item ties each stream back to its media description. Implementations MUST support the RTCP SDES item method and SHOULD support the RTP header extension method for carrying RtpStreamId. A stream uses only one alternative rid-id at a time but MAY change format, and rid-id, packet by packet.

An endpoint with a simulcast source can send up to the negotiated number of streams. A stream might not be continuously sent, for example because it is paused, because of sender logic, or because of lack of network resources, but every negotiated stream keeps an active SSRC, at least in regular RTCP reports.

The RFC then describes middlebox behavior. A media-switching mixer produces one stable RTP stream per its own media source, switching among incoming simulcast streams and rewriting header fields. A selective forwarding middlebox maps one simulcast stream onto one RTP stream per media source towards the receiver. Switching video needs suitable switching points, and Full Intra Requests are commonly used to ask for one.

Bitrate for all simulcast streams of a source is bounded by any SDP b= line on that media description. When bandwidth falls, the order on the a=simulcast line suggests which streams to prioritize, and pause-capable streams of little use can be paused.
sections.eli5: Each copy of the video wears a name tag so the receiver knows which copy it is. If the road gets crowded, the sender drops the least important copies first.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The simulcast attributes are vulnerable to attacks on signaling. Falsely adding a=simulcast can cause extra RTP streams that would otherwise not be sent. The effect is limited because all streams of a media description share its bandwidth, but many unwanted streams can eat into the share of the stream that was wanted. Hostile removal of the attribute just means simulcast is not used.

Integrity protection and source authentication of all SDP signaling can mitigate these risks. The security aspects of a=rid and the RtpStreamId item are covered in RFC 8851 and RFC 8852, and this RFC adds no further concerns.
sections.eli5: If someone sneaks extra lines into the order form, you might get lots of copies you did not want. Keeping the form sealed and checked stops that.

messages.label: a=simulcast:send 1;2,3 recv 4
messages.note: Offers two streams to send (the second with alternatives 2 and 3) and wants one stream back.

messages.label: a=simulcast:recv 1;2 send 4
messages.note: Reverses the directions and removes the alternative rid-id 3.
